content: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has significantly reduced both the morbidity and mortality associated with HIV/AIDS. In resource-limited settings, a common first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimen typically includes a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) combined with two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs). However, when treatment failure occurs, transitioning to a second-line therapy becomes necessary. This systematic review was conducted to determine the most effective antiretroviral regimen for patients with HIV who experience virologic failure on a first-line ART regimen recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). To achieve this, electronic databases and conference proceedings were searched using relevant terms, without restrictions on language. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving HIV-infected adolescents and adults who were administered second-line ART after failing a first-line regimen. Observational studies were also included due to the limited number of RCTs available. The primary outcome assessed was mortality, while secondary outcomes included the rate of adverse events, changes in mean CD4 cell count, clinical resolution of symptoms, the proportion of patients achieving undetectable viral load (VL), and the acquisition of genotypic mutations. Two independent reviewers evaluated studies for inclusion based on predefined criteria, and data were extracted using a standardized form. The risk of bias in individual studies was assessed, and the GRADE approach was applied to evaluate the overall quality of evidence. One randomized trial involving 136 patients investigated whether maintaining lamivudine (3TC) in second-line regimens affected virological outcomes. The study found no significant difference in virological suppression between patients who continued lamivudine and those who did not. Additionally, two small observational studies, reported in abstract form, also found no difference in the proportion of patients achieving viral suppression after six months or in the time to HIV-1 RNA suppression when comparing regimens containing lamivudine or emtricitabine (FTC) to those that excluded these drugs. No trials were identified that directly compared the efficacy of boosted protease inhibitors (PIs) or different nucleoside backbone combinations in patients who failed first-line therapy with non-thymidine analog regimens. However, observational studies conducted in resource-limited settings suggest that short-term virological responses to boosted PI-based regimens are promising. In conclusion, there is limited high-quality evidence to guide the selection of second-line therapies for patients with HIV who fail first-line treatment with a WHO-recommended regimen. The available data, including one randomized trial and two low-quality observational studies, suggest that maintaining lamivudine in second-line regimens does not significantly impact virological suppression. While boosted PI-based regimens appear to yield favorable outcomes, no studies have directly compared different boosted PIs in second-line settings. Current treatment recommendations are therefore based on available resources, as well as individual patient and public health considerations.
